--- title: "Research proposal overview" engine: knitr --- The structure and paragraph ranges below are planning tools: adapt them to the research problem, the evidence available, and the scope of the proposal. ::: {.callout-note title="Use the assignment prompt first"} The proposal is assigned and evaluated by your professor, not by this guide. Follow any required sections, length, format, or evaluation criteria supplied by the professor. The structure below helps you and your mentor develop and organize the scientific content when the assignment leaves those decisions open. Paragraph ranges and section labels are starting points, not requirements to reproduce. ::: ## Research proposal structure: The big picture 1. **Introduction** -- 4-7 paragraphs: Why you are doing your study and the QHPT a. **Umbrella statement** -- 1 paragraph: This paragraph provides the scope of your study while orienting the reader to the broad context of your study and why it is important. The first sentence should establish the broad problem and give the reader a reason to continue. b. **Literature review** -- 1-3 paragraphs: This provides the context for your study. What do readers need to know in order to be able to interpret your research question and hypotheses? Without stating your research question, what is the conceptual framework of your study (what do we already know)? What have other researchers done to address your area of interest? Include species- or location-specific information when it is necessary for the argument, but do not let natural history or local description replace the broader conceptual framework. See [Synthesizing the literature](literature_review.qmd). c. **Conceptual holes in our understanding** -- 1-2 paragraphs: Which aspects of your area of interest remain unexplored or underexplored? What are the lingering questions or conflicts within the literature? Focus specifically on the "holes" that you intend to address with your QHPT (without stating your QHPT). The *holes* should represent a meaningful limitation in our understanding. Repeating a study in a nearby place becomes a gap only when that change in context could alter the process or interpretation. d. **Q**uestion, **H**ypothesis, **P**rediction, **T**est -- 1 paragraph: i. **Question**: The big-picture uncertainty being addressed. Questions are derived from theory and the literature and represent an important idea that advances your field of study. When useful, state a broadly applicable conceptual question and then explain how your study organism and location provide an appropriate system in which to address it. Some projects require explicitly system-specific questions. Clarity and alignment matter more than following a grammatical rule. ii. **Hypotheses**: These are potential mechanistic answers to the question, derived from theory and the literature. A strong scientific hypothesis explains how or why the phenomenon occurs. Write directional comparisons between predictor and response variables as predictions. Describe theoretically sound, tractable, and relevant alternatives when more than one mechanism could answer the same question. Statistical hypotheses are formal claims about quantities or distributions and should not be substituted for the scientific explanation. iii. **Predictions**: If a hypothesis and the assumptions linking it to your system are reasonable, what observable pattern do you expect? What result would be difficult to reconcile with the proposed mechanism? Be sure to support the expected pattern with theory and literature. *Note: A strong quantitative prediction can often be plotted, suggests directionality, and has a clear predictor and response variable.* iv. **Tests**: These represent the statistical and experimental "nuts and bolts" that describe how your predictions will be evaluated with the data. Stay big picture here (you will describe this in more detail in the methods). v. **Implications**: 1-2 sentences that offer a strong, but reasonable and accurate, statement about why your project is the most important project *ever* (i.e., how will it contribute to our understanding of the issue). Tie the content back to the "holes in our understanding" and umbrella statement. Content should also include (and sometimes be framed as) broader benefits to your research program and society at large. 2. **Methods** -- What you will do in your study and how the procedures relate to your QHPT Use [Planning and writing a methods section](methods_planning.qmd) to organize the methodological decisions that you work out with your mentor, flag unresolved details, and transfer TREAT to methods paragraphs. a. **Study area and site selection** -- 1 paragraph: i. Describe your study region (i.e., the extent of your study) and why this region is appropriate for addressing your research question and hypothesis. ii. If location data are used, describe how the locations were selected (if a subset of available locations) within the context of the research question, hypothesis, and prediction. For example, if I'm exploring the influence of historic redlining policies on current socioeconomic distributions, and I choose to study Baltimore, MD, and Durham, NC, I need to justify my choice of those cities and describe how this choice provides the opportunity to test my prediction. b. **Study design, sampling, data sources, and measurements**: Describe what will be observed, how observations will be selected, where the data will come from, and how the important concepts will be measured. Separate these jobs into paragraphs when combining them would make the procedure difficult to follow. c. **Data preparation**: Describe steps that materially change the meaning, scale, or comparability of the data. Mundane wrangling steps (e.g., "I will mutate the data frames to add a column") should not be included. d. **Analysis**: Framing each analysis as a test of a prediction, describe the predictor, response, comparison, and output that will be interpreted. If you are proposing to apply a model, describe the assumptions and limitations that materially affect inference. 3. **Research timeline**: What you expect to do in each phase of the project. Be sure to include any deliverables at each phase, if applicable. 4. **Literature cited** ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Now you!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} **Place the information** **1.** Where does this material primarily belong? > Relationships between foliage density and nest survival vary among species and habitats.
**2.** Where does this material primarily belong? > We will compare daily predation risk across the observed foliage-density gradient while accounting for nests grouped within study sites.
::: ## General notes on proposal writing - Be sure that your proposal follows the inverted-pyramid writing format. Scientific topics are often complex and require high expertise in your subject matter to understand. Your reviewers will often not have expertise in your area of study. Structuring your writing from broad to specific will help reviewers understand your system. Do so across and within paragraphs. - Most reviewers are nerds that often care (too?) deeply about a topic other than your own. Their priorities may differ from yours. *Do* share your passion, and make an airtight case that your study system and method for addressing it is important. - Avoid value judgments and generalizations. We often speak/write in coded generalizations on the assumption that our peers agree with us (e.g., that invasive species are bad). In your writing, be conscious that reviewers may not share your values. - Cite literature accurately! You need to read every paper that you cite and be sure that you adequately understand what was written. Citation accuracy protects both academic integrity and your credibility with reviewers who may know the studies well. For example, I have peer-reviewed manuscripts that misrepresented my own research! - Some reviewers are keen on poking holes in your methods (I am often one of those). Even without detailed knowledge of your subject matter, they may know the ins-and-outs of sampling methodology or the statistical analyses that you're proposing. Be sure to develop and explain your methods clearly and accurately. - The structure is adaptable. Some proposals use different section headings or require additional elements, but the central work remains the same: make the logic visible, support the gap, and explain how the proposed methods test the predictions. ## Common pitfalls The most general pitfall is beginning to draft before the argument has been outlined. More specific checks now appear in [Synthesizing the literature](literature_review.qmd) and [Gap hunting](gap_hunting.qmd). For examples of strong and weak introductions, see [Learning from published introductions](introduction_examples.qmd). ::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="Make a writing outline prior to writing!"} Avoid freewriting -- it is a great way to waste a lot of valuable time! We strongly recommend creating a detailed outline with your own material **before** writing your proposal. :::
